entries.text: To get a good understanding of this example, you will need to be familiar with the :man:`readv(2)` system call. If you aren't familiar with it, I suggest you read `a more gentler <https://unixism.net/2020/04/io-uring-by-example-part-1-introduction/>`_ introduction and then return back here to continue.

lines: Scatter reads first
``readv`` fills an array of ``std.posix.iovec`` ranges in sequence. Each range
has a mutable byte pointer and a length. A successful call can fill only part of
the combined capacity; zero bytes means end of input. Never print every allocated
byte merely because a buffer exists.
The synchronous program establishes the byte-preservation contract before
introducing ring publication. It streams through two 2048-byte ranges, retries
interrupted calls and writes exactly the returned count.
Linux syscall reference
These Linux ABI entry points are exposed by ``std.os.linux``. Unlike Zig's
``IoUring`` methods, raw syscalls return errno-encoded ``usize`` values. Decode
with ``linux.errno(result)`` before casting a successful descriptor or count.
They do not set a libc ``errno`` variable or return a Zig error union.

``IOSQE_FIXED_FILE``
Interpret SQE ``fd`` as a registered-file table index.
``IOSQE_IO_DRAIN``
Hold this request until prior work completes and order later work behind it,
subject to the kernel's drain rules. Different from a dependency chain.
``IOSQE_IO_LINK``
Link to the next SQE; the first entry without the bit ends the chain. An
unsuccessful/unexpected result can cancel the remaining unstarted members
with ``-ECANCELED``. Unrelated requests/chains remain independent.
``IOSQE_IO_HARDLINK``
Preserve a submitted chain across completion-result failures; submission
failure can still break it. Do not require a separate soft-link bit to use
the kernel's hard-link semantics.

lines: An asynchronous ``prep_files_update`` restores the original descriptor. Its
separate CQE reports **one updated entry**, not zero. Only after that CQE does the
next read use the restored entry. Replacing slot 1 with ``-1`` and unregistering
the table each make later fixed-file reads fail with ``-EBADF``. The JSON report
contains actual tags/results/flags and byte arrays, not padded buffers. This
sequential example does not establish safety for racing table updates and I/O.

lines: ``REGISTER_FILES`` takes a ``linux.fd_t`` array and count. Fixed-file SQEs set
``IOSQE_FIXED_FILE`` and put a table index in ``fd``. ``-1`` creates a sparse entry
where supported. ``REGISTER_FILES_UPDATE`` takes a native
``linux.io_uring_files_update`` containing a table offset and descriptor pointer;
``nr_args`` counts replacements. ``UNREGISTER_FILES`` takes null/zero.
``IoUring.register_files_update`` handles that ABI structure synchronously.
``sqe.prep_files_update`` instead prepares an asynchronous update request, with
its own CQE. Table references and process descriptor ownership are different;
closing a process descriptor is not the same as unregistering a table entry.
Release resources only after their dependent requests finish.

The :ref:`reader <cat_zig>` has one outstanding request. A copy can overlap a
read for one range with a write for another. This example keeps two stable
16-KiB slots and submits a batch when work is available. Its origin is Shuveb
Hussain's tutorial, based on the
`fio copying example <https://github.com/axboe/fio/blob/master/t/io_uring.c>`_.
The implementation here is native Zig 0.17.0.
